This guide names each kind of test in the repository, when to use it, and a real example to copy. The rules that apply to every change are in

A pure function, formatter, parser, or one module's contract.
An ecosystem detector reads a manifest, or a registry rule/schema changes.
A detector's shared guarantees: determinism, locations, evidence, valid fields, bounded inputs, zero findings, malformed input.
A rule or detector has positive/negative boundaries that belong in a reviewable repository on disk.
The behavior crosses the process boundary: arguments, exit codes, stdout, JSON contracts.
A tool, resource, prompt, or annotation changes; use the in-memory transport.

Any parser that reads untrusted repository content.
A budget or evaluator changes, or a measured fixture needs a smoke run.
Repository guardrails, corpus thresholds, or the harness that compares findings with ground truth.
Use a unit test for a pure function or one module's contract. It is the cheapest kind and should carry most of the logic coverage. Assert the public result, not internal calls.
The scan engine's ordering rule is a unit test too:
builds two findings out of order, runs
, and asserts the IDs come back sorted. That is the observable contract; do not assert on how the sort is implemented.
Detector tests read a small repository and assert findings: rule ID, severity, location, and evidence. Use the fixture directories for stable boundary cases, and a
repository when the input is specific to the test.

, an HTTP source, a versioned PURL, a duplicate ID) and asserts both the validator and the error message that names the rule and field. When you add a validation rule, add a row to that table instead of a new test function.
Use detector tests when the question is "does this ecosystem produce the right finding at the right line"; use registry tests when the question is "can this rule shape exist at all".

Conformance is the shared harness every detector must pass: deterministic ordered output, locations that exist, authoritative evidence, findings with valid fields, bounded inputs, no findings on a zero-finding fixture, and no throw on malformed input. It lives in
is the one suite every registered detector runs. It reads

, so registering a detector adds it automatically, and it generates an empty repository, a repository whose every declared input is malformed, and one at the limits of the input, depth, and size checks. When the detector has

, a copy of those fixtures is also scanned and its findings checked for valid fields, evidence, existing locations, and stable order. Write an explicit expected-findings test in the detector's own file for what it reports; the shared suite checks how every detector reports.

Use conformance when you add a detector, change the SDK seam, or change a guarantee that applies to all detectors. The negative tests in the same file show the failure you are buying protection from: a detector whose ordered output changes between scans (
), reports a location that does not exist, or omits a source. Do not duplicate these checks in an individual detector test.

Use a fixture when the boundary should stay visible in review, when the same input is scanned more than once, or when a maintainer triage decision needs to be locked in. Use an inline

Use an end-to-end test when the behavior only exists across the process boundary: parsing arguments, exit codes, stdout/stderr, and the JSON document a user or script consumes.

Do not use an end-to-end test to check logic that a unit test can reach. Spawning the CLI is justified when the wiring itself is the thing that can break.
MCP tests use the SDK's in-memory transport, so no port, subprocess, or network is involved.

Use an in-memory MCP test for any tool shape, resource, prompt, or annotation change. Use the stdio test only when the transport or entry point changes.
Action tests keep two boundaries apart. Pure renderers and evaluators get unit tests; the pull-request behavior gets a stubbed GitHub API and a local bare
remote, so the test proves the branch and request without touching github.com.

shows the evaluator unit style: fixed measurements, exact boundary, and one millisecond past it. Use the stub when the behavior is "what request does the Action make"; use the evaluator test when the behavior is "what counts as a violation".
Every parser that reads repository content belongs in the fuzz suite.

runs a property over arbitrary strings and a grammar-flavored hostile input set. The property is stronger than "does not crash": the same input must produce the same result twice, and no single input may exceed the time budget.

Keep the evaluator and the measurement apart. The evaluator is deterministic and gets boundary tests; the measured run gets a generous budget so it catches a catastrophe without failing on runner noise.
